title: Core beliefs in Islam
description: What every Muslim believes: the oneness of God (tawhid), the six articles of faith, and what those beliefs change about an ordinary day.

sections.heading: Tawhid: the oneness of God
sections.content:
**Tawhid** is the belief in the absolute oneness of Allah (God). It sits at the center of Islam, and every other part of the faith rests on it. When you said the Shahada, **"La ilaha illallah, Muhammadur Rasulullah"** (There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah), tawhid is what you affirmed.

Tawhid means Allah is one, unique, and without partners. He was not born and has no children. Nothing in creation resembles Him, and His essence is past what a human mind can hold, though you can come to know Him through His names and attributes. One entire surah is given to this: **Surah Al-Ikhlas** (Chapter 112) says, "Say, He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is born, nor is there to Him any equivalent."

If you came to Islam from another faith tradition, tawhid can feel like a weight coming off. All of your worship and reliance goes to one place. There is no intermediary and no saint to pass your prayers through, so your relationship with Allah is direct and personal.

Tawhid also changes ordinary decisions. No person, no possession, and no job title deserves the devotion that belongs to Allah alone. That takes the pressure off trying to please everyone, and off chasing things that were never going to satisfy you. Your footing stops depending on how the week is going.

sections.heading: Worshipping Allah alone
sections.content:
People come to Islam from every background, and the next section covers faiths other than Christianity. If you grew up Christian, you may have loved Jesus (peace be upon him) all your life, and you do not have to stop. Muslims honour him as one of the greatest prophets. The Quran describes him saying, **"Indeed, I am the servant of Allah"** (19:30, translation of meaning), and he called people to worship God alone.

The first half of the Shahada, "there is no god worthy of worship except Allah", turns that into daily practice. In every prayer you say, **"It is You we worship and You we ask for help"** (1:5). Surah Al-Ikhlas (112) describes the One you worship: Allah, the Eternal Refuge, who neither begets nor is born, with nothing equal to Him.

What this changes in practice:

- You pray to Allah directly, and your personal dua can be in English or any language.
- Prayer and worship go to Allah alone: not to Jesus, Mary, saints or angels, not to the Prophet Muhammad, and not at graves.
- Nobody has to pass your prayers on for you. Allah hears you.

Giving any worship to someone besides Allah is called **shirk**, and the Quran treats it very seriously: **"Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills"** (4:48). That verse is about where you are heading, not a reason to punish yourself over the past. The Quran says past wrongs are forgiven for those who stop (8:38), and the Prophet said that Islam wipes out what came before it (Sahih Muslim 121). What you did before Islam is forgiven.

**Things you owned before Islam.** A Bible or other religious books can stay on your shelf: a SeekersGuidance answer says owning them is not sinful in itself, and borrowed copies go back to their owner. For crosses, statues and family heirlooms, ask a teacher before you do anything, and never destroy something that matters to your family. The Quran tells Muslims not to insult what others worship (6:108).

**Worship is different from being with your family.** Sitting with your family at a meal, visiting over the holidays, or looking after a relative is keeping family ties, which the Quran asks of you (31:15 and 60:8). Joining in prayers or a religious service directed to anyone other than Allah is the part you step out of.

**Church weddings and funerals.** Scholars answer this differently, and it is fine to ask before you decide:

- Egypt's Dar al-Ifta and an AMJA scholar say you may attend a relative's funeral, even in a church, as part of keeping family ties.
- SeekersGuidance answers from the Hanafi school allow the family gathering but advise against attending the church service itself without a strong need.
- IslamQA takes a strict view, including on attending a church wedding.

None of these answers has you join in worship, and all of them fit the Quran's call to keep treating your family kindly. Your situation matters, so ask a local imam or scholar you trust before the event. Our holidays and family occasions guide has scripts for these conversations.

sections.heading: If you come from another faith or from no religion
sections.content:
Much of what new Muslims read assumes a Christian upbringing. In a 2025 Yaqeen Institute survey of 618 converts in the United States, 60% were raised Christian. About 19% grew up with no religion, and about 20% came from Jewish, Buddhist, Hindu or other traditions. So roughly two in five did not start from Christianity.

The principle is the same for everyone. Your worship goes to Allah alone, and your family still gets your kindness and company (31:15 and 60:8). The Quran also tells Muslims not to insult what other people call on besides Allah (6:108), so there is no need to mock your family's gods to prove you are sincere.

**A shrine or statues at home.** We did not find a scholarly answer written for a new Muslim living in a family home with a shrine. The closest is a Shafi'i answer from SeekersGuidance (Shaykh Jamir Meah) about a temporary stay in a friend's home where the main objects had been put away. It says staying in a room with statues is disliked in the reliable Shafi'i view, while another Shafi'i view says it is not allowed, and it advises staying clear where you can. Other schools were not checked. Do not break or hide family property, and ask a teacher about your own home.

**Food offered in worship (prasad and similar).** A SeekersGuidance answer by Mawlana Ilyas Patel, using Hanafi reasoning, says food offered at a temple in the name of someone other than Allah is not eaten. Decline it politely. If you are handed some by mistake, the answer says you may give it to a non-Muslim. Ordinary family cooking is a separate question, covered in the halal living topic.

**Karma and rebirth.** Islam agrees that deeds have results: **"So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it"** (99:7-8). A SeekersGuidance answer by Ustadh Abdullah Anik Misra explains that Islam does not teach rebirth or an impersonal law of karma. There is one life, and every outcome is from Allah.

**Yoga and meditation.** Shaykh Faraz Rabbani (SeekersGuidance) writes, **"When yoga is practiced purely for the element of physical exercise, then there is no harm in it."** The meditative and spiritual parts are left out.

**Smudging and Indigenous ceremonies.** A SeekersGuidance answer by Shaykh Irshaad Sedick says burning sage for its smell or for health is fine, but smudging done for spiritual protection clashes with relying on Allah. That answer was not written with First Nations, Inuit or Metis communities in mind. Your identity and your family's culture stay yours. For questions about particular ceremonies, talk to a teacher, and if you can, to Indigenous Muslims who have faced the same questions.

**Ancestor rites and family graves.** We did not find a named scholarly answer on ancestor rites such as incense at family graves or Qingming. Keep caring for your family and for your relatives' graves, and ask a teacher before the next family rite.

**Festivals such as Diwali, Vaisakhi, Lunar New Year, Nowruz and Hanukkah.** The holidays and family occasions guide explains the line between family time and worship, with what we found for each festival.

**Coming from no religion.** Talking to a God you have only just come to believe in can feel strange. The Prophet said every child is born on the fitrah, a natural inclination to recognise God (Sahih al-Bukhari 1385; see also 30:30). You can talk to Allah in your own words, in any language.

**Coming from a Jewish background.** Moses (Musa) and the Torah are honoured in Islam, and much of what you know about the prophets will be familiar. The sections further down on prophets and on Jesus, Mary and the earlier scriptures explain where Islam agrees and where it differs.

A few practical steps:

1. Tell your family you still love and respect them before you explain what you will step out of.
2. Decide before the next family rite what you will do: attend without taking part, help with the food, or visit before or after.
3. Ask a local imam about the exact festival or rite in your family.

sections.heading: The six articles of faith
sections.content:
Muslims hold **six articles of faith (arkan al-iman)**. Together they are what **iman** (faith) actually consists of:

**1. Belief in Allah:** One God, the Creator, Sustainer, and Sovereign of everything that exists. Allah has names and attributes that tell you who He is: the Most Merciful, the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, the Just, and more. Learning Allah through those names is some of the most rewarding study you will do.

**2. Belief in the angels:** Angels are beings Allah created from light who carry out His commands. Jibreel (Gabriel) brought the Quran to the Prophet Muhammad, Mika'il (Michael) is responsible for rain and sustenance, and other angels record your deeds, protect you, and will be present on the Day of Judgment. Angels do not have free will the way humans do, and they worship Allah without pause.

**3. Belief in the divine books:** Allah sent scriptures to guide people throughout history. They include the scrolls of Ibrahim (Abraham), the Torah given to Musa (Moses), the Zabur (Psalms) given to Dawud (David), the Injil (Gospel) given to Isa (Jesus), and finally the Quran given to Muhammad (peace be upon them all). Muslims hold that the Quran is the final, preserved revelation, confirming and completing the messages before it.

**4. Belief in the prophets and messengers:** Allah sent prophets to every nation to call people back to the truth. Muslims believe in all of them, from Adam to Muhammad, including Nuh (Noah), Ibrahim (Abraham), Musa (Moses), and Isa (Jesus). Muhammad (peace be upon him) is the final prophet, and his message is for all of humanity.

**5. Belief in the Day of Judgment:** There will be a day when everyone is raised and held accountable for what they did. Those who lived righteously are rewarded with Paradise, and those who rejected the truth and kept to wrongdoing face the consequences. This is why your choices matter past this temporary world.

**6. Belief in qadar (divine decree):** Allah knows everything that has happened and everything that will happen. Nothing occurs outside His knowledge and permission. This does not cancel human free will, and you are still answerable for your choices. What it does mean is that you can trust there is wisdom in how things unfold, even when you cannot see it. For many people this is the article of faith that carries them through the hardest stretches.

sections.heading: Understanding Allah's names and attributes
sections.content:
Learning **Allah's names and attributes** is one of the steadiest ways to grow in faith. Knowing the names goes past memorising the words. It means understanding what they mean and letting them shape how you live.

A few of the names tend to matter most to new Muslims:

- **Ar-Rahman** (The Most Gracious) and **Ar-Raheem** (The Most Merciful). These two open almost every surah in the Quran. Allah's mercy covers everything. Whatever sits in your past, His mercy is larger than it.
- **Al-Ghaffar** (The Repeatedly Forgiving). Allah does not forgive once and then stop. He forgives again and again, which is worth knowing while you are new and still making mistakes.
- **Al-Wadud** (The Most Loving). Allah loves His creation and loves those who turn to Him. Love belongs in your relationship with Him alongside awe.
- **As-Sabur** (The Patient). Allah is patient with His creation and gives people time and chances to come back to Him.
- **Al-Hakeem** (The All-Wise). There is wisdom behind everything Allah decrees, even when that wisdom is not visible to us yet.

Many Muslims take one name at a time and sit with its meaning through the day. You might keep **Ar-Rahman** for a week and watch for where mercy shows up in your life. After a while the names stop being vocabulary and start being something you have actually felt.

The names between them cover every human need. When you are afraid, Allah is **Al-Muhaymin** (The Protector). When you feel lost, He is **Al-Hadi** (The Guide). When money is short, He is **Ar-Razzaq** (The Provider).

sections.heading: Prophets in Islam
sections.content:
Muslims believe Allah sent prophets and messengers to every nation through history, and all of them carried the same core message: worship the one true God and live righteously. The Quran names **25 prophets**, while indicating there were many more.

If you come from a Christian or Jewish background, many of these names will already be familiar. Adam, Noah (Nuh), Abraham (Ibrahim), Moses (Musa), David (Dawud), Solomon (Sulayman), and Jesus (Isa) are all honored prophets in Islam. Reading their stories from the Islamic side is worth doing slowly, since some details match what you grew up with and some do not.

A few things to hold onto about prophets in Islam:

- **All prophets taught tawhid**, the oneness of God. The core message never changed. What changed were the specific laws and practices, updated for different times and peoples.
- **Prophets were human beings.** They ate, slept, had families, and went through hardship. Their humanity is the point, because it means you can actually follow their example.
- **Prophets were protected from major sins.** They were the best of their people and divinely guided, though still human, and small errors were possible.
- **Muhammad is the final prophet.** Muslims hold that no prophet comes after Muhammad (peace be upon him). His message, kept in the Quran and in his teachings (Sunnah), is for everyone until the end of time.

The stories of the prophets carry lesson after lesson about patience, trust in Allah, and courage under pressure. New Muslims often find the story of Ibrahim (Abraham) the most comforting one, because he had to leave everything familiar behind to follow Allah's guidance. If that sounds close to where you are standing right now, you are reading it correctly.

The Quran says: **"We have not sent you (O Muhammad) except as a mercy to the worlds"** (21:107). That verse is how Muslims see the Prophet Muhammad: a mercy, and a guide for all of humanity.

sections.heading: Jesus, Mary and the earlier scriptures
sections.content:
If your family is Christian or Jewish, these are often the first questions they ask. Here is what Muslims believe, in words you can share.

**Jesus (Isa).** Muslims love and honour Jesus, peace be upon him. The Quran calls him the Messiah, a messenger of Allah and His word given to Mary (4:171), and says he is honoured in this world and the next (3:45). Muslims do not believe he is God or the son of God: the same verse says Allah is one God, far above having a son (4:171).

**Mary (Maryam).** A whole surah of the Quran carries her name. The Prophet (peace be upon him) named her among the best of women (Sahih al-Bukhari 3432).

**The cross.** The Quran says Jesus was not killed and was not crucified (4:157). This is a real difference from Christian belief. Say it gently, and only when someone asks. The Prophet also said that Jesus son of Mary will come down again and judge with justice (Sahih al-Bukhari 3448).

**The Torah and the Gospel.** Muslims believe Allah gave the Torah to Moses and the Gospel (Injil) to Jesus, with guidance and light (5:46). For what is in the Bible as it is read today, the Prophet taught Muslims neither to confirm nor to deny the reports of Jews and Christians, and to say, "We believe in Allah and what is revealed to us" (Sahih al-Bukhari 4485).

**Reading the Bible yourself.** A SeekersGuidance answer by Shaykh Abdul-Rahim Reasat says reading it may be permissible if you understand your own belief well and are not prone to doubts, and advises against going online to look for problems in it. It is usually better left for later, with a teacher.

**Talking with your family.** The Quran tells Muslims to speak with Jews and Christians "in a way that is best" and to say, "our God and your God is one" (29:46). Start with what you still share: belief in God, the prophets, Mary and Jesus. Answer one question at a time and offer to come back to the rest. Leave arguments about Bible manuscripts for later study with a teacher. Debate videos are not a script for talking with people you love, and nobody in your family needs to hear that they are bad people. Yaqeen Institute's article "Who is Jesus in Islam?" is a good next read.

sections.heading: The afterlife and accountability
sections.content:
Belief in the afterlife runs through the whole of Islamic faith. This worldly life is temporary: a test, and a chance to grow closer to Allah through worship and doing right by people. The lasting life comes after this one.

The afterlife has several stages:

**The life of the grave (Barzakh):** After death the soul enters a state called Barzakh, a realm in between this life and the Day of Judgment. The righteous find peace and comfort there, while those who rejected the truth may find difficulty.

**The Day of Judgment (Yawm al-Qiyamah):** All of creation is gathered before Allah. Every person is shown their deeds, good and bad, and judged with perfect justice. The Quran describes that day in close detail and keeps returning to one point: nothing is hidden from Allah.

**Paradise (Jannah) and Hellfire (Jahannam):** Those who believed and lived righteously enter Paradise, a place of lasting joy, peace, and closeness to Allah that no description quite reaches. Those who rejected faith and kept to wrongdoing face Hellfire. Allah's mercy is vast, though, and He forgives whom He wills.

Accountability can feel sobering and motivating at the same time. It means your life has a purpose and your choices land somewhere. Every act of kindness, every prayer, every moment of patience counts. Hold that next to hope in Allah's mercy rather than carrying it on its own. The Quran keeps pairing its warnings with reassurance: **"My mercy encompasses all things"** (7:156).

This belief is here to give life direction, not to make you anxious. Once you know this world is not all there is, the pressure to squeeze every bit of happiness out of it comes off. Hardship gets easier to sit with because it has an end. And you can do good quietly, without anyone noticing, because Allah already saw it.

sections.heading: Qadar: understanding divine decree
sections.content:
**Qadar** (divine decree or predestination) is the article of faith people ask about most, and the hardest of the six to state simply. Qadar means Allah has complete knowledge of everything, past and present and future, and that nothing happens outside His knowledge and permission.

There are four parts to it:

1. **Allah's knowledge:** Allah knows everything that has happened, is happening, and will happen. His knowledge is complete and perfect.
2. **Allah's writing:** Everything is recorded in a preserved tablet (Al-Lawh Al-Mahfuz).
3. **Allah's will:** Nothing happens in creation except by Allah's will.
4. **Allah's creation:** Allah is the Creator of everything, including our actions.

**"But what about free will?"** Fair question, and a very common one. Islam teaches that humans have genuine free will and make real choices. You decide whether to be honest or dishonest, whether to pray, whether to be kind or cruel, and you answer for those decisions. Qadar does not make you a puppet. It means Allah, in His infinite knowledge, already knows what you will choose, and He still leaves the choosing to you.

Think of a teacher who knows a student well enough to predict exactly how they will answer a question. The teacher knowing does not make the student answer that way. The student still answers freely. Allah's knowledge is far beyond any teacher's, but the same principle holds: knowing a choice in advance does not remove it.

**Believing in qadar changes how loss feels.** When you lose a job, or get sick, or get turned down, you can rest on the fact that there is wisdom in it even if none of that wisdom is visible yet. And when things go well, gratitude comes more easily than swagger.
